baby-toddler-juice-fruit-and-vegetable.title: Baby Toddler Juice, Fruit and Vegetable

content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Juice is a 100 % natural drink made from selected fruits and vegetables, specially formulated for children aged 6 months to 3 years. It contains no added sugar, preservatives, or artificial flavors. The juice supports the development of taste preferences and provides essential vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The juice is produced by cold‑press extraction, preserving most of the nutrients.
It combines apple, carrot, pear and spinach – a blend rich in beta‑carotene and vitamin C.
Each package features a QR code that reveals the origin of the ingredients when scanned.
The product has passed independent testing for pesticide residues and heavy metals.
Its mild sweetness and smooth texture make the transition from breast milk to solid foods easier.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and enhances iron absorption from plant foods.

items.title: Contains beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is converted to vitamin A, which is important for vision and cell growth.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber from the fruits and vegetables promotes healthy bowel movements.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: The juice contains no added sugars, helping to establish healthy eating habits early.

items.title: Allergy to fruit components
items.content: Children with known allergies to apple, pear, or carrot should be evaluated by a pediatrician before introducing the product.

items.title: Not suitable for infants under 6 months
items.content: Babies younger than 6 months should receive only breast milk or specialized infant formula.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Once opened, the juice should be consumed within 24 hours and kept refrigerated to prevent microbial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the juice in small portions (30–60 ml) from a clean bottle or cup. Gently shake before serving to evenly distribute any sediment. It can be mixed with a small amount of baby puree for flavor variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened packages in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the juice refrigerated and use within one day. Discard if the smell, color, or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Parmesan is a hard Italian cheese made from cow's milk. Dry grated Parmesan is used as a flavorful topping, giving dishes a nutty, slightly sweet taste and a distinctive aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Parmesan holds a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status and can only be produced in specific regions of Italy.
Grated Parmesan is a staple in Italian cuisine for sprinkling over pasta, risotto, and soups.
The cheese is aged a minimum of 12 months, often 24–36 months, which deepens its flavor.
Parmesan provides more than 30 % protein, making it a valuable source of protein.
Grated Parmesan stores well in an airtight container and retains its aroma for a long time.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Parmesan contains about 1,100 mg of calcium per 100 g, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Approximately 35 g of protein per 100 g helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains phosphorus and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for energy metabolism and immune function.

items.title: Low lactose
items.content: Extended aging reduces lactose levels, making Parmesan more tolerable for those with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or milk proteins may react to Parmesan.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Grated Parmesan contains about 650 mg of sodium per 100 g, so those with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Approximately 430 kcal per 100 g, so consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sprinkle grated Parmesan over pasta, risotto, soups, salads, and casseroles. It can be added directly before serving or used as a fragrant base during cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry grated Parmesan in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from light. For longer storage keep it in the refrigerator, and for extended shelf life, in the freezer.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicory beverage is a non‑alcoholic drink made from the dried roots of the chicory plant (Cichorium intybus). It has a mildly bitter, coffee‑like flavor and is often used as a caffeine‑free coffee substitute or a flavorful soft drink.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicory is cultivated in Europe, North America and Russia; roots are harvested in the autumn.
During World War II chicory became a popular coffee substitute in Europe due to coffee shortages.
High in inulin, the drink is naturally sweet without added sugar.
Chicory has a long history in traditional medicine for supporting digestion and liver health.
Dried chicory roots can be stored for up to two years in a dry, dark place.

items.title: Rich in inulin
items.content: Inulin is a prebiotic fiber that promotes the growth of beneficial gut bacteria and improves digestive health.

items.title: Low caffeine content
items.content: The beverage contains no caffeine, making it suitable for people who avoid stimulants.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Chicory contains polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports liver function
items.content: Extracts of chicory root are traditionally used to aid liver detoxification and function.

items.title: May help regulate blood sugar
items.content: Inulin can slow glucose absorption, contributing to more stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to chicory.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large amounts of inulin can cause gas, bloating, and diarrhea.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Chicory may enhance the effects of diuretics and blood‑sugar‑lowering drugs.

items.title: Pregnancy and lactation
items.content: Pregnant or nursing women should consult a healthcare professional before consuming.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicory beverage can be enjoyed hot or cold, diluting a concentrate with water or milk. It is often used as a base for coffee‑style drinks, smoothies, and dessert sauces. Sweeteners, spices (cinnamon, vanilla) or cream can be added to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried chicory roots in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Prepared beverage should be kept in the refrigerator and consumed within 3‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Meringue cookie is a light, crisp treat made from egg whites, sugar, and a touch of starch. The mixture is whipped into a stiff foam and baked at low temperature, giving the biscuit its characteristic airy, melt‑in‑the‑mouth texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meringue originated in France in the 17th century and was first used as a decorative element for desserts.
Sugar not only sweetens the meringue but also stabilizes the protein foam, allowing it to hold its shape during baking.
The cookies can be flavored with vanilla, lemon zest, cocoa powder, or spices.
Thin meringue sheets are often used in pastry cakes as a “crystalline” layer.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Because most of the mass is egg white and sugar, meringue cookies contain far less fat than typical baked goods.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Egg whites provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Meringue is naturally free of gluten, making it suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Since the main ingredient is egg white, meringue can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with egg allergies.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: The large amount of sugar gives meringue a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to tooth decay and weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Meringue cookies can be enjoyed on their own, used as a base for layered cakes, as a garnish for ice cream, incorporated into chocolate fondues, or broken into pieces and topped with fresh berries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store meringue cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption, which makes them soft.

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with sauce and meat is a school‑lunch dish consisting of boiled pasta, a tomato‑based sauce, and pieces of boiled or stewed meat. The meal provides energy and nutrients needed by children for a school day.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Short‑shaped pasta such as shells or penne is commonly used in school cafeterias because it holds sauce well.
The sauce is usually made from tomatoes, onion, carrot and a small amount of vegetable oil, providing vitamin C and beta‑carotene.
Meat is typically beef or chicken, cut into small pieces for easy chewing by children.
Pasta is one of the most popular items on school menus worldwide.
The dish scales easily: a single large batch can serve hundreds of students.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta supplies a steady release of energy, helping maintain blood‑sugar levels throughout the school day.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat in the sauce adds complete protein needed for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomato sauce provides vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium, while the meat contributes iron and zinc.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Durum‑wheat pasta contains dietary fiber that promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of carbs and protein helps children feel full longer.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat pasta contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains added salt; excess sodium may be a concern for children with hypertension.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Improperly cooked or low‑quality meat can harbor bacteria, so proper cooking temperatures are essential.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some schools use preservatives or flavor enhancers; those with sensitivities should check the ingredient list.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The dish is served hot in portion trays. Children can use a fork or spoon, mixing the pasta with the sauce so each piece is coated. Grated cheese may be added if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared pasta with sauce and meat should be kept refrigerated at +2…+4 °C for no more than 24 hours. For longer storage, freeze in airtight containers and reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken soup is a classic dish made from chicken meat, bones, vegetables, and spices. It has a gentle aroma, light texture, and comforting flavor, often served as a starter in cold weather.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken broth is the base for many cuisines, including French, Chinese, and Russian.
Traditionally the soup includes carrots, onion, celery, and noodles or rice for added heartiness.
Some cultures add ginger or garlic to boost its immune‑supporting properties.
Chicken soup is often called a “home remedy” for colds because of its warming and hydrating effects.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The chicken meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of collagen
items.content: Simmered bones and cartilage release collagen, supporting joint and skin health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup supplies vitamins B6 and B12, important for the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Electrolytes
items.content: Salt and vegetables deliver sodium and potassium, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Warm liquid aids hydration, especially during illness.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Over‑salting can raise blood pressure; monitor added salt.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to chicken meat or eggs used in the recipe.

items.title: Contamination
items.content: Undercooked bones may harbor pathogens; simmer the broth for at least 1–2 hours.

items.title: Histamine formation
items.content: Prolonged storage can lead to histamine buildup, causing food reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often garnished with herbs, lemon wedges, noodles, rice, or potatoes. Fresh vegetables or scallions can be added for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomatoes are the edible fruits of the tomato plant (Solanum lycopersicum), native to South America. They have a juicy, slightly sweet‑tart flavor and a characteristic bright red color. Raw tomatoes are eaten fresh and are also used in salads, sauces, soups, and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes belong to the nightshade family and are botanically classified as berries, though they are culinarily treated as vegetables.
The heaviest recorded tomato weighed over 3.5 kg.
Lycopene gives tomatoes their red hue and acts as a powerful antioxidant.
There are more than 10,000 tomato varieties, differing in shape, size, taste, and color.
Tomatoes were first cultivated by the Aztecs and spread worldwide after the Columbian exchange.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes provide a high amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is a potent antioxidant that may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and certain cancers.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports proper heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Tomatoes are low in calories but high in water and fiber, promoting satiety.

items.title: Provides vitamin K1
items.content: Vitamin K1 is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes, such as skin itching or swelling.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: Unripe (green) tomatoes contain solanine, which can be toxic in large amounts; they should be avoided or cooked.

items.title: Food interactions
items.content: Tomatoes may enhance the effect of certain blood thinners due to their vitamin K content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw tomatoes can be sliced for salads, sandwiches, or enjoyed as a snack with a pinch of salt and olive oil. They are also diced for salsa, added to pasta sauces, soups, and casseroles. For optimal flavor, let sliced tomatoes sit for a few minutes after seasoning.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tomatoes at room temperature, away from direct sunlight, to allow them to ripen. Once fully ripe, they can be placed in the refrigerator for a few days, though this may affect texture. Avoid airtight containers, which can trap moisture and cause spoilage.
